Anyway, here is my 2cents...
I don't think diet failures have much to do with the physiological side of things. Insulin resistance and sensitivity are both real phenomenon, but that's not where I think the real problem is. It's all about the mind. When I found out that I was the problem (and not my genes or the dryer that shrinks my clothes or whatever) it hurt me. It sucks to feel responsible for being miserable. I got angry, depressed. It would have been much easier to turn the truth down, and blame it on my knee pain or my genes. It took me some time to fully understand that I was victimizing myself by blaming everything around me, and that I was the only person that could solve my problem. After I let that sink in, I started eating whole foods and low Cal options, weighting my food, etc etc. My mood got better, then my self image got better, and finally my physical image improved.
I gave myself some tough love. I went to the gym when I didn't feel like it. I went to bed hungry. I had to make some "tough" decisions between a Cal dense burger and a low Cal stir fry. I feel like it was a part of undoing all the wrong that I did to myself. The longer the abuse, the tougher the "purging" time. It was very empowering. I get to decide when I stop losing weight.I get to pick the right food for my body. I'm to blame if I don't see any progress.

IMO, the feeling of empowerment is what makes someone successful in dieting. There is no self-empowerment if you follow a crash diet because a granny smith apple and a piece of salmon make magical fat burner soldiers. There is empowerment in deciding to have blueberries instead of ice cream or having poached chicken over a few snags for your own well being, however. It's not about being on a diet... Through my eyes, it's about knowing how much calories your body needs, then picking the best aliments to fill this need. By claiming insulin is the source of obesity, I feel like it removes the very important feeling of responsibility, followed by some self-love, self-respect, and empowerment from the process. Even if it's not the first intention, using insulin spike/sensitivity as an ultimate cause might end up being a crotch to lean on, or some sort of excuses for the more stubborn obese.
